results.name: above_vs_below_range
results.description: Among non-example targets 1-10 from the nearest example and outside the examples' range, yes rate for targets above the max example minus targets below the min example; observed above null means people extend generalisation upward more than downward relative to the symmetric-distance model, below null means downward bias.
results.code:
# name: above_vs_below_range
# description: Among non-example targets 1-10 from the nearest example and outside the examples' range, yes rate for targets above the max example minus targets below the min example; observed above null means people extend generalisation upward more than downward relative to the symmetric-distance model, below null means downward bias.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    valid = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    dist = np.where(valid, np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), np.inf)
    nearest = dist.min(axis=1)
    nonmember = nearest > 0
    lo = np.where(valid, ex, np.inf).min(axis=1)
    hi = np.where(valid, ex, -np.inf).max(axis=1)
    base = nonmember & (nearest >= 1) & (nearest <= 10)
    a = r[base & (t > hi)]; b = r[base & (t < lo)]
    if len(a) == 0 or len(b) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(a.mean() - b.mean())

results.name: inside_range_far
results.description: Among non-example targets more than 5 from the nearest example, yes rate for targets inside the examples' [min,max] range minus targets outside it; observed above null means people generalise over the interval spanned by the examples more than the model (which has no range/interval property), below null means less.
results.code:
# name: inside_range_far
# description: Among non-example targets more than 5 from the nearest example, yes rate for targets inside the examples' [min,max] range minus targets outside it; observed above null means people generalise over the interval spanned by the examples more than the model (which has no range/interval property), below null means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    valid = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    dist = np.where(valid, np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), np.inf)
    nearest = dist.min(axis=1)
    nonmember = nearest > 0
    lo = np.where(valid, ex, np.inf).min(axis=1)
    hi = np.where(valid, ex, -np.inf).max(axis=1)
    far = nonmember & (nearest > 5)
    inside = (t > lo) & (t < hi)
    a = r[far & inside]; b = r[far & ~inside]
    if len(a) == 0 or len(b) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(a.mean() - b.mean())

results.name: cell_unanimity
results.description: Fraction of (set, target) cells with >=2 responses in which all responses agree; observed above null means responses are more deterministic/extreme (closer to 0 or 1 per item) than the model's graded posterior predicts, below null means more disagreement.

results.name: set_breadth_spread
results.description: Standard deviation across example sets (with >=20 responses) of each set's mean yes rate; observed above null means sets differ in how broadly people generalise more than the model predicts (some sets near-zero, others very broad), below null means less.

results.name: consistent_last_digit_far
results.description: For sets of >=2 examples that all share one last digit, yes rate among non-example targets more than 5 from every example that end in that same digit; observed above null means people adopt the crisp shared-final-digit rule and extend it to distant numbers more than the model's graded profile predicts, below null means less.
results.code:
# name: consistent_last_digit_far
# description: For sets of >=2 examples that all share one last digit, yes rate among non-example targets more than 5 from every example that end in that same digit; observed above null means people adopt the crisp shared-final-digit rule and extend it to distant numbers more than the model's graded profile predicts, below null means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    valid = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    dist = np.where(valid, np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), np.inf)
    nearest = dist.min(axis=1)
    nonmember = nearest > 0
    ld = np.where(valid, np.mod(ex, 10), np.nan)
    ld0 = ld[:, 0]
    allsame = (n >= 2) & (np.nansum(ld == ld0[:, None], axis=1) == n)
    m = allsame & nonmember & (nearest > 5) & (np.mod(t, 10) == ld0)
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0

results.name: near_gradient_1_vs_2to5
results.description: Among non-example targets, yes rate at distance exactly 1 from the nearest example minus yes rate at distance 2-5; observed above null means human generalisation is concentrated on immediate neighbours more steeply than the model's fitted neighbourhood width predicts, below null means flatter.
results.code:
# name: near_gradient_1_vs_2to5
# description: Among non-example targets, yes rate at distance exactly 1 from the nearest example minus yes rate at distance 2-5; observed above null means human generalisation is concentrated on immediate neighbours more steeply than the model's fitted neighbourhood width predicts, below null means flatter.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    valid = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    dist = np.where(valid, np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), np.inf)
    nearest = dist.min(axis=1)
    nonmember = nearest > 0
    a = r[nonmember & (nearest == 1)]
    b = r[nonmember & (nearest >= 2) & (nearest <= 5)]
    if len(a) == 0 or len(b) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(a.mean() - b.mean())

results.name: outlier_example_neighborhood
results.description: For sets of >=3 examples where exactly one example breaks the majority last digit, yes rate among non-example targets within 3 of that outlier example that do not end in the majority digit; observed above null means people treat the exceptional example as a genuine member and generalise around it (e.g. 27 -> 20s) more than the model, which discounts it as noise.
results.code:
# name: outlier_example_neighborhood
# description: For sets of >=3 examples where exactly one example breaks the majority last digit, yes rate among non-example targets within 3 of that outlier example that do not end in the majority digit; observed above null means people treat the exceptional example as a genuine member and generalise around it (e.g. 27 -> 20s) more than the model, which discounts it as noise.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    valid = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    dist = np.where(valid, np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), np.inf)
    nearest = dist.min(axis=1)
    nonmember = nearest > 0
    ld = np.where(valid, np.mod(ex, 10), np.nan)
    cnt = np.zeros((len(t), 10))
    for d in range(10):
        cnt[:, d] = (ld == d).sum(axis=1)
    maj = cnt.argmax(axis=1)
    majc = cnt.max(axis=1)
    is_out = valid & (ld != maj[:, None])
    dout = np.where(is_out, np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), np.inf).min(axis=1)
    m = (n >= 3) & (majc == n - 1) & nonmember & (dout <= 3) & (np.mod(t, 10) != maj)
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0

results.name: first_vs_last_proximity
results.description: For multi-example sets, yes rate among non-example targets within 3 of only the first-shown example minus those within 3 of only the last-shown example; nonzero observed vs null near 0 means presentation order matters (positive = primacy, negative = recency), which the order-invariant model cannot produce.
results.code:
# name: first_vs_last_proximity
# description: For multi-example sets, yes rate among non-example targets within 3 of only the first-shown example minus those within 3 of only the last-shown example; nonzero observed vs null near 0 means presentation order matters (positive = primacy, negative = recency), which the order-invariant model cannot produce.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    valid = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    dist = np.where(valid, np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), np.inf)
    nearest = dist.min(axis=1)
    nonmember = nearest > 0
    last = n - 1
    idx = np.arange(len(t))
    d_first = dist[:, 0]
    d_last = dist[idx, last]
    nearc = (dist <= 3).sum(axis=1)
    m = nonmember & (n >= 2) & (nearc == 1)
    a = r[m & (d_first <= 3)]; b = r[m & (d_last <= 3)]
    if len(a) == 0 or len(b) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(a.mean() - b.mean())
